items.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: And we did a Christmas album in the late 90s. I mean we’re still friends.

ctx.x: A meeting. After I did “I Love the Night Life” the next person to call me was Clive Davis and flew me to New York and he quizzed me. He played me demos of songs. He’d play me records that they were getting ready to release. And he would be very specific. “Do you think this is a hit? Why or why not?” He was very specific and we were there hours the first time I met with Clive in New York. And we left after that first day and he said, “Put together some songs” he’s a song man to this day, he’s what 86 or so now,…

successful, and her second album. And we did a Christmas album in the late 90s. I mean we’re still friends. I just went to see her play a few months ago, a couple of months ago. We’re still great friends. But that’s usually how — you have to meet with them ahead of time to see if there’s a chemistry.
What’s the first run through of the songs like? Do you have a piano player on hand or did you play your guitar?

items.title: Buckingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2019
items.q: it was on a Melissa Manchester Christmas album and I had Eddie Gomez flying to Nashville from New York

ctx.x: I think so. I don’t know any singer I ever worked with — well no, I can tell you a couple. When I produced Dionne Warwick’s albums for Clive Davis, Dionne had gone, she was a a music teacher. And we were doing a session one day, it was a Michael McDonald song that must have had dozens of chord changes in it and oh, it was fast. I can’t even remember the name of the song. And I had the best guys. And the guitarist that day was Larry Byron from Muscle Shoals. Larry had played with Steppenwolf at one time, and then…

Michael McDonald’s demo and there it was. One note in a chord was a half a step off. You know, it was supposed to be — instead of a seven it was supposed to be a flat seven or a major seven — some note was a half a step off. So there is an example of somebody who did go to school. That’s the only singer I can think of off the top of my head, that went to school, and subsequently she took us to school that day. But most — I can’t think of any other singers who were schooled like that. Maybe some jazz singers or…
That’s funny, if you took the written notes to Nashville and they convert it to the number chart.
